PMDD symptoms occur during the luteal phase and, by definition, are limited to ovulatory menstrual cycles. C
SSRIs treat the affective and somatic symptoms of PMDD. A

Other potentially effective treatments are oral contraceptives, B calcium, B chasteberry, B and cognitive behavioral therapy. B

background.definition: Premenstrual dysphoric disorder (PMDD) is a depressive disorder characterized by severe and disabling symptoms of irritability, anger, internal tension, dysphoria, and mood lability that interfere with work, school, social activities, and relationships. PMDD symptoms occur during the luteal phase and, by definition, are limited to ovulatory menstrual cycles. Premenstrual symptoms occur along a continuum with PMDD at the most severe end of the spectrum and isolated symptoms at the least severe. Premenstrual syndrome (PMS) is a term commonly used by laypersons to describe symptoms experienced to varying degrees by many women before menses onset. To diagnose PMS, patients should have at least 2 symptoms (one affective and one somatic).

list.listitem: In a community-based sample of 1488 women between the ages of 12 and 24 years, 5.8% met criteria for PMDD. A similar percentage was found in a French population study of 2863 reproductive-aged women; 4.1% of women qualified for severe PMS (6 symptoms) and 8.1% reported 1 to 5 PMS symptoms that impacted their daily lives.
In a year-long population-based study in a Swedish university hospital, among 2318 women delivering infants, 7.1% had a history of PMS and 2.9% had a history of PMDD.

Among 75 Polish female athletes, aged 16 to 22 years, and 50 healthy, controls not practicing competitive sports, the prevalence of PMDD was similar at 9.33% and 6%, but PMS was significantly more frequent among athletes (49.33% vs. 32%).
The highest prevalence rate of 17.6% was reported from a retrospective community cohort of 727 young adult women aged 18 and 24 years in Brazil.
Eighteen percent to 31% of women meet criteria for PMS.
One study showed an increase in direct medical costs of $59 per year per woman with PMDD and indirect costs to employers (eg, lost workdays) of $4333 per year per woman with PMDD.
Ninety percent of cases remain undiagnosed.
Women who seek treatment for PMDD see an average of 4 physicians over a 5-year period before diagnosis.
Women with PMDD have an average of 6.4 days of severe symptoms per cycle, which amounts to nearly 3000 days (>8 years) of symptoms during their reproductive period.
Based on a study of 66 women with untreated PMDD, patients were expected to experience a quality-adjusted life-year loss of about 3 years during their lifetime.

In a European and Latin American population study of 4085 subjects, up to 35% of women of reproductive age were moderately or severely affected in activities of daily living by cyclical premenstrual symptoms.

There is significant mental-health comorbidity in women with PMDD. Thirty percent to 76% of women diagnosed with PMDD have a lifetime history of depression compared with 15% of women of similar age without PMDD. There is also an association between a history of PMDD or PMS and the development of self-reported postpartum depression.

Women with PMDD also have an increased bipolar disorder. Women with comorbid PMDD and bipolar disorder, in one study, were found to have earlier onset of bipolar illness, higher rates of rapid cycling, and increased number of past-year hypo/manic and lifetime/past-year depressive episodes compared to women with bipolar disorder without PMDD. Comorbid PMDD was also associated with higher prevalence of panic disorder, post-traumatic stress disorder, generalized anxiety disorder (GAD), bulimia nervosa, substance abuse, and adult attention deficit disorder.
In the Brazilian cohort study, PMDD was significantly associated with current major depression disorder, agoraphobia, bipolar disorder, current suicide risk, GAD, social phobia, and specific phobia.
The etiology of PMDD is unknown. However, hormonal disturbances and physiologic mechanisms are being studied.
Twin studies show a high concordance of symptoms. However, authors of a recent literature review on the genetic basis of PMDD found limited supporting evidence for the commonly studied genes.

There are several theories of the pathophysiology of PMDD: (1) genetic (because of a higher concordance in identical twins than in fraternal twins), (2) sensitivity to progesterone, (3) ovarian hormones producing adverse effects in susceptible women via their actions on serotonin and γ-aminobutyric acid, and (4) disturbed aldosterone activity and functional hyperprolactinemia.

There is also evidence that the GABAergic neurotransmitter system is involved; in one small study, GABA concentrations were significantly lower in mood-related brain regions of women with PMDD compared to healthy controls. In addition, allopregnanolone, a positive modulator of the GABAA receptor, is a provoking factor for negative mood symptoms in PMDD and its isomer, isoallopregnanolone, may ameliorate PMDD symptoms, based on an RCT.

In one study, blocking the conversion of progesterone to its 5α-reduced neurosteroid metabolite with high-dose dutasteride resulted in significant reduction in several core PMDD symptoms, but had no effect on mood in control women.
The diagnosis is made based on daily prospective symptom ratings by the patient and possibly someone living with her. C
The diagnosis of PMDD requires 5 symptoms with at least 1 being a core mood symptom. Symptoms must be severe enough to interfere or cause dysfunction within occupational and social domains. C

Differential.Differential_Features: Bothersome adverse somatic and/or affective symptoms occurring during the luteal phase
Depressed mood for most days for at least 2 years; not related to the menstrual cycle
At least 5 symptoms of depressed mood most of the day nearly every day with significant impairment; not related to the menstrual cycle
Excessive anxiety and worry more days than not for at least 6 months
Mood disturbance not related to menstrual cycle
4 pain symptoms, 2 GI symptoms other than pain, 1 sexual symptom, and 1 pseudoneurological symptom
Recurrent episodes of binge eating with compensatory behavior at least twice weekly for 3 months
Personality disturbance not related to menstrual cycle
Fatigue, depressed mood, swelling, weight gain; symptoms present throughout the menstrual cycle
Lack of energy, concentration difficulties, depressed mood, present throughout the menstrual cycle
Muscle or joint pain, fatigue, depressed mood; symptoms can be worsened by the menstrual cycle but persist throughout the cycle
Swelling, weight gain, bloating; symptoms present through the menstrual cycle

list.listitem: Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders (DSM)-5 criteria: 5 or more of the following symptoms have been present most of the time during the last week of the luteal phase, start to improve within a few days after onset of menses, and become minimal or absent in the week post-menses. At least 1 of the symptoms is from the first 4 listed: (1) feeling sad, hopeless, or self-deprecating; (2) feeling tense, anxious, or "on edge"; (3) marked lability of mood interspersed with frequent tearfulness; (4) marked irritability, anger, and increased interpersonal conflicts; (5) decreased interest in usual activities; can be associated with withdrawal from social situations; (6) difficulty concentrating; (7) feeling fatigued, lethargic, or lacking in energy; (8) marked changes in appetite that may be associated with binge eating or craving certain foods; (9) hypersomnia or insomnia; (10) subjective feeling of being overwhelmed or out of control; (11) physical symptoms, such as breast tenderness or swelling, headaches, or sensations of "bloating" or weight gain, with tightness of fit of clothing, shoes, or rings.
There may also be joint pain or muscle pain and the symptoms may be associated with suicidal thoughts.
Symptoms should be present for most months during the previous 12 months and must be confirmed using prospective daily symptom ratings for 2 consecutive months.
Symptoms can’t be attributable to a substance or another medical condition.

In the DSM-5, PMDD was moved from DSM-IV Appendix B, “Criteria Sets and Axes Provided for Further Study”, to a full category in the main body of DSM-5. In addition, prospective diagnosis should be performed in two symptomatic but not necessarily consecutive cycles.

PMDD can occur at any age after menarche, with a peak incidence around age 35 years. Symptoms worsen until relieved by menopause. The symptoms of PMDD are of similar severity to those of other independent mental disorders and cause impairment in the ability to function socially or occupationally in the week prior to menses.

Use the history and physical examination to distinguish PMDD from general medical conditions that are being exacerbated by the menstrual cycle. Ask about affective symptoms (eg, depression, anger, anxiety, irritability, confusion, social withdrawal) and somatic symptoms (eg, breast tenderness, abdominal bloating, headache, swelling of the extremities, sleep disturbance, weight or hair changes, joint or muscle pain).

Symptoms should occur exclusively during the week before menses during ovulatory cycles, not premenarche, postmenopausal, pregnancy-related, or postoophorectomy. Onset and cessation of symptoms may fluctuate from cycle to cycle by 4 or more days after the onset of menses. Symptom severity should include any amount of impaired function at work, school, in usual activities, or with relationships.
In one self-identified cohort of women with PMDD, mood and physical symptoms were most severe and disabling in the 4 days before through the first 2 days of menses.

Take a menstrual history to include onset, last menstrual period, frequency, flow, pregnancies. Also review the past medical history for anemia, thyroid disease, medications, psychiatric illnesses (including postpartum depression), and suicidal thoughts.

The family history should focus on premenstrual symptoms and psychiatric illnesses, while the social history should review smoking, alcohol use, and drug use; caffeine intake; diet; stressors; abuse; educational level; and work.
Focus the physical examination on potential alternate diagnoses by looking for pallor, goiter, hair and skin dryness, edema, weight changes, joint swelling/warmth/effusion.

Patients should be asked to keep a daily symptoms diary for 2 consecutive months to include symptom type, severity, and functional impairment along with the menstrual history. Options include the Daily Record of Severity of Problems (24 items), the Premenstrual Symptom Screening Tool (19 items), the Calendar of Premenstrual Experiences (22 items), and the Penn Daily Symptom Report Scale.

Symptom clusters have been identified that appear stable for individual women. In one study of diaries of 174 women with PMDD or severe PMS, 6 symptom clusters were identified using factor analysis - affective dysphoria, somatic dysphoria, irritability, breast/body sensitivity, pain, and eating behavior; somatic dysphoria was the cluster most strongly associated with impairment in work, relationships or recreation.
There are no tests that are diagnostic for this condition and no tests that are routinely recommended for all patients with suspected PMDD.

Laboratory testing to exclude underlying medical conditions when suspected based on the clinical history and physical examination include thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) (hypothyroidism), hemoglobin (anemia), serum creatinine (renal failure, if there is swelling or hypertension), ANA or RF (joint symptoms), electrolytes (if bulimia or renal insufficiency suspected), hormone levels (if perimenopausal symptoms are present), and serum prolactin (if there is headache or galactorrhea).

Consider PMDD in women of reproductive age with affective or somatic symptoms occurring during the week prior to their menstrual cycles. The diagnosis is made using daily prospective symptom ratings by the patient and possibly someone living with her.

Routine diagnostic testing is not recommended, although you may consider a complete blood count, a TSH test, and testing the serum creatinine level, markers for collagen vascular disease, serum prolactin level, or hormone levels if clinically indicated based on symptoms.
Consider other comorbid mental-health conditions and assess suicide risk.
See for a suggested approach to management.
Treatment is based on severity and types of symptoms. Treatment should begin with lifestyle modification, relaxation, exercise, and possibly cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT). C
If the patient does not respond to the above measures, prescribe an SSRI to be taken during the luteal phase. A
If luteal phase treatment is inadequate, prescribe continuous SSRI therapy. A
Oral contraceptives containing drospirenone may be effective for physical, mood, and behavioral symptoms. B
Consider alternative therapies such as chasteberry, calcium, or magnesium. B
In refractory cases, suppression of ovulation can be achieved with use of gonadotropin-releasing hormone agonists or surgery (total abdominal hysterectomy with bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy). C
See for a summary of the medical management of PMDD.

SSRIs are effective in treating the affective and somatic symptoms of PMDD; fluoxetine hydrochloride, paroxetine controlled release, and sertraline hydrochloride are Food and Drug Administration-approved for PMDD. Paroxetine was also found to significantly improve social functioning in patients with PMDD, as was venlafaxine. Authors of a recent systematic review of 55 studies found SSRIs and low doses of oral estrogen/progestins most effective for patients with PMDD who had no other mental disorders.

The onset of action with SSRIs for PMDD is shorter than when treating for depression. Treatment with SSRIs limited to the premenstrual phase is as effective as continuous treatment; however, in 1 study, physical symptoms were improved only with sertraline dosed continuously. In another small study of 12 women, treatment with fluoxetine significantly improved VAS scores for irritability, sadness, anxiety, and mood swings starting on the second day of luteal phase treatment.
OCs may be effective for PMDD, although data are conflicting and include high response rates for placebo.

OCs containing drospirenone, a derivative of spironolactone with antimineralocorticoid and antiandrogenic properties, appear effective for severity of physical, mood, and behavioral symptoms; other OCs have mixed or minimal efficacy with some improvement in bloating and breast pain but no improvement in mood symptoms.Common side effects of nausea, intermenstrual bleeding, and breast pain were more likely for the drospirenone combined OC groups (COC). In the longest trial (2-year), women in the drospirenone COC group had similar premenstrual symptoms to the comparison group given desogestrel 150 µg plus ethinyl estradiol 30 µg (OR 0.87; 95% CI, 0.63-1.22); rates of adverse events were similar.

In a multicenter placebo-controlled RCT of 367 women with PMDD, women randomized to continuous daily levonorgestrel 90 mcg/ethinyl estradiol 20 mcg had a significantly lower Daily Record of Severity of Problems (DSRP) score compared to women on placebo at the late luteal phase. Other primary end points were not significantly different between groups.

Estradiol implants and patches appear effective for symptom control. Authors of a Cochrane review of 5 RCTs found low-quality evidence of a small to moderate effect on global PMS symptom scores of continuous oestrogen (transdermal patches or subcutaneous implants) plus progestogen.
Progesterone was not found to be effective in multiple studies.

GnRH agonists for suppression of ovulation are effective for irritability and depression but they should only be used for short-term treatment in patients with severe symptoms because of side effects. A 6-month trial is recommended with estrogen add-back therapy prior to considering hysterectomy. Danazol is also moderately effective for treating physical and mood symptoms but is limited by side effects. Anxiolytic agents may be used in selected patients during the luteal phase for refractory anxiety symptoms.

In a small pilot study of 20 women, the addition of the atypical antipsychotic quetiapine (Seroquel) to SSRI therapy appeared useful in improving mood symptoms when there was an inadequate response to therapy.

In a phase II study of 106 women with PMDD, subcutaneous Sepranolone, a GABAA modulating steroid antagonist, administered every second day during the luteal phase was superior to placebo during one menstrual cycle for reducing total DRSP score (75% reduction and 47% reduction, respectively). No adverse effects were reported.
Total abdominal hysterectomy and bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy is an option for women who have debilitating PMDD and fail other therapies.
Selected herbal therapies may be helpful for symptom control. A systematic review of Chinese herbal medicines specifically found only limited data to support their efficacy.

Vitex agnus-castus (chasteberry) is effective for mood symptoms. Authors of two systematic reviews confirmed positive effects on PMS/PMDD symptoms, but trials were associated with a high risk of bias and limitations included different definitions of diagnostic criteria, different outcome measures and different chasteberry preparations used.
Vitamin B6 is useful for depressive symptoms.
Vitamin D may be useful for reducing mood PMS symptoms in adolescents with severe hypovitaminosis D.
Calcium carbonate supplementation was found to be effective, particularly for negative affect, water retention, food cravings, and pain.
Magnesium was found to be useful after 3 months for breast tenderness, swelling of extremities, and abdominal tenderness.
A well-designed RCT found that saffron was effective for PMS.
Homeopathy, selected based on a prognostic questionnaire and electronic algorithm, was more effective than placebo in mean reduction in DRSP score at 4 months in an RCT of 60 women with PMS/PMDD.

Acupuncture may be helpful for premenstrual symptoms but data quality is poor. Authors of a Cochrane review of 5 low- to very-low-quality trials with 277 women found improvement in PMS physical and psychological symptoms of PMS compared to a sham control.

CBT can help patients develop coping mechanisms; in one RCT, CBT was as effective as fluoxetine, although slower to achieve a response. In a meta-analysis of low quality RCTs, CBT reduced anxiety (NNT = 5), and depression (NNT = 5), and had a possible beneficial effect on behavioral changes (NNT = 4) and symptoms of daily living (NNT = 4). The combination of medical treatment with CBT did not show an additional improvement in symptoms.

Internet-based 8-week therapist-guided CBT was more effective at 6 months than wait listing on functional and psychological impairment, impact on everyday life, symptom intensity, and symptom disability in an RCT of 174 women with PMDD. Addressing stress and coping strategies may be important as lower levels of perceived stress were associated with stronger improvement in functional impairment and higher levels of active coping were associated with stronger improvement in interference in everyday life and symptom intensity.
The use of symptom charts can help patients with coping and in planning activities around symptom days.
See for treatment options.

Regular aerobic exercise can have positive effects on physical and emotional components of the disorder, possible because of the release of endorphins, but there are insufficient data for making recommendations for women with PMS/PMDD.
A reduction in the intake of caffeine, refined sugar, and alcohol can decrease anxiety and irritability.
Limit sodium to decrease edema and bloating.
Patients with PMDD should consider continuing treatment (unless pregnant) until the onset of menopause.

In patients with severe PMS, the relapse rate was lower for women treated with sertraline for 1 year versus 4 months (see Prognosis). There was no effect of treatment duration on relapse for women with mild symptoms.
PMDD is a relatively stable and enduring condition requiring monitoring and treatment until menopause. B

If PMDD is left undiagnosed and untreated, it can have a profound influence on the patient's personal and professional life, leading to a loss of work days, decreased productivity, and a severe strain on personal relationships.
The underlying condition is likely to continue to be present and women should consider continuing treatment until menopause, unless pregnant.

In a study of patients with severe PMS, the relapse rate was lower for women treated with sertraline for 1 year versus 4 months (41% vs. 60%, respectively) with a longer median time to relapse for women treated for one year (8 months vs. 4 months; hazard ratio, 0.58; 95% CI, 0.34-0.98). Patients who demonstrated remission were least likely to relapse.
In a French population study, among women who qualified for PMS during 1 or both years of the study, 72% demonstrated fluctuation in their PMS status over a 1-year follow-up period.
The patient should be seen 2 cycles after the initial consultation to evaluate symptom logs and confirm the diagnosis; these logs should be continued to monitor treatment effectiveness.
After initiation of treatment, recheck patients after the next menstrual cycle then after 1 or 2 more cycles until the patient is improved and stable.

Clinical judgment should be used in determining the follow-up interval after starting or changing dosages of medication. One-month follow-up for side effects and adherence is recommended following the initiation of SSRIs.

algorithm.title: Premenstrual Dysphoric Disorder: Diagnosis and Treatment.

cell.label: Patient with signs/symptoms of PMS/PMDD. Perform history and physical examination. Have patient perform symptom assessment for 2 cycles.
Suspected underlying medical or psychology condition.
Evaluation as indicated (CBC, TSH, hormone levels, screening for psychiatric disorders).
Patient education lifestyle modification, CAM treatment. Improvement?
Lifestyle modification, CAM treatment, consider luteal-phase (cyclic) SSRI. Improvement?
Treat symptoms individually (eg, anxiety with benzodiazepine); consider ovulatory suppression with drospirenone OC or GnRH agonist; consider TAH/BSO as last resort.

footnotes.footnote: Abbreviations: PMDD, premenstrual dysphoric disorder; PMS, premenstrual syndrome; CAM, complementary/alternative medicine; SSRI, selective serotonin receptor inhibitor; OCP, oral contraceptive pill; GnRH, gonadotropin releasing hormone; TAH/BSO, total abdominal hysterectomy/bilateral oophorectomy.

feature.caption: Treatment Options for Premenstrual Dysphoric Disorder.
feature.feature_body:
Treatment Dosage Comments
Psychological
CBT
Single trial found it to be as effective as fluoxetine
Natural remedies
Vitamin B6 100 mg/day Improves depressive symptoms
Magnesium 360 mg 3 times daily during luteal phase* Improves physical symptoms (eg, breast/abdominal tenderness, swelling)
Chasteberry 30-40 mg/day during luteal phase Decreases symptoms
Calcium 1200-1600 mg/day Decreases symptoms (eg, negative affect, water retention, food craving, pain); can improve bone health
Pharmacotherapy
Venlafaxine 25-50 mg twice daily Only continuous treatment studied
Fluoxetine 20-80 mg/day Effective for tension, irritability, dysphoria
Sertraline 50-150 mg/day or 100 mg daily during luteal phase* Effective for behavioral and emotional symptoms
Oral contraceptives containing drospirenone Daily Effective for physical, mood, and behavioral changes
Clomipramine 25-75 mg/day Used for refractory symptoms
Alprazolam .5-2 mg 3 times daily during luteal phase* Used for refractory anxiety symptoms
Surgical treatment
Oophorectomy
Effective as last resort
*Luteal phase treatment begins on day 14 of the menstrual cycle until the onset of menses.
